title: 01 Vectors and Linear Transformations: Visual Guide
outline: Title: 01 Vectors and Linear Transformations: Visual Guide

1. The Linearity Test | The bridge. Side by side: the function test you already know on one number line (f(x) = 3x, 3x + 2, x^2) and the identical two-line test on arrows in the plane (T(x, y)). Two sliders move the inputs and each of the three laws - additivity, homogeneity, and where the origin lands - is recomputed and marked MATCH or DIFFERENT live. | The definition of linear did not change when the input became an arrow; only the input did. Affine rules like 3x + 2 fail because the origin moves, and x^2 shows a fixed origin is necessary but not sufficient - which is why two answers, T(e1) and T(e2), written as columns, are enough to store the whole rule.

2. Add, Scale, Dot | Vector operations on a drawn plane. Sliders set the components of u and v and a scalar c; the SVG draws u, v, the tip-to-tail dashed copy that produces u+v, and the scaled arrow c*u sliding along the line through the origin. Pills read off u+v, u-v, c*u, u.v, both lengths, and the angle. | Addition and scalar multiplication are component by component and return arrows; the dot product returns a plain number. Its sign is the angle: positive acute, zero perpendicular, negative obtuse - and |u| = sqrt(u.u) is the same operation pointed at itself. A zero vector makes the angle undefined but the dot product still 0.

3. Where The Basis Goes | Four sliders are the four matrix entries, presented as the two questions they actually answer: where e1 goes and where e2 goes. The unit square, its image, both basis images and a test vector are drawn live, with presets for identity, rotate 90 degrees, reflect across the x-axis, shear by 2 and scale x by 2, and a live name for the transformation. | The columns of a matrix ARE the images of the basis vectors, so T(v) = x*col1 + y*col2 and matrix-vector multiplication is a combination of columns rather than a rule to memorise. The origin never moves. The shear and the horizontal scaling send (2, 1) to the same place, which is why the unit square, not a favourite test vector, identifies a transformation.

4. Rows Dot, Columns Combine | The same product Ax computed two ways, toggled: row reading (each output entry is one dot product of a row with the input) and column reading (the output is x copies of column 1 plus y copies of column 2, drawn tip to tail). Below it, four sliders set the shapes of A and B and the panel rules on whether AB is defined and what shape it has. | Both readings give the same answer: rows are how you compute, columns are how you think. Every entry of any matrix product is a dot product, which forces the shape rule - columns of A must equal rows of B, the inner pair, because a dot product needs two lists of the same length - and the outer pair survives as the shape of the result.

5. Order Changes Everything | Pick which of rotate, shear, reflect happens first and which second. Three panes show the unit square at the start, after the first transformation, and after both; the product matrix is computed live alongside the reverse-order product, and tapping any of its four entries expands the single dot product that produced it. | Multiplying matrices composes transformations into one. BAx means B(Ax), so the matrix nearest the vector acts first and the written order reads right to left, chronologically. Swapping the order generally changes the transformation: composition is associative but almost never commutative.
